Triggers.value: Night-time or waking up in the dark

Maladaptive Strategies.value: I drink alcohol, take medication or use drugs

vignette:
Evan had been working late at his apartment in a downtown loft when the incident happened, long after his divorce had become a quiet fact of his life and his freelance graphic design work had taken on the same isolated, screen-lit rhythm each night. He had stepped outside just before midnight to clear his head, cutting through a nearly empty parking lot toward his car. In the dim light, a police vehicle pulled in beside him and, in the confusion of the moment, the officers approached quickly with their uniforms, flashlights, and weapons visible. What unfolded in those first seconds was so abrupt and disorienting that Evan later struggled to explain it in a way that felt complete; he remembered the dark lot, the harsh beams of light, the sound of authoritative commands, and the overwhelming certainty that he was in danger. The experience left him feeling exposed and trapped, as if there had been no safe way to understand what was happening before it was already upon him.

In the weeks after, Evan found that night itself had become a difficult place to be. Waking in the dark jolted him into immediate tension, and he would lie still for a moment before turning on a lamp, needing the room lit before he could orient himself again. He noticed the same tightening when he was outside after sunset and when he had to cross an unlit stretch of street from his apartment to his car. He did not describe this as fear of darkness in the abstract so much as a dread that settled in at the exact moment he could not see clearly enough to know what was around him. Similar cars brought the event back with a force that surprised him. A sedan with emergency-style headlights or a vehicle parked at an angle like the one that had pulled in beside him could catch his attention instantly, and he would feel himself scanning the driver, the rear seat, the mirrors, waiting for some sign that he was about to be approached again. Crowded places carried a different but equally painful strain. Grocery stores, sidewalks at rush hour, and packed bars made him feel hemmed in, unable to tell who was near him or where he might move if he needed to get away. Even before he entered a crowded space, he would picture the crush of bodies and the loss of room to breathe.

Over time, Evan began arranging his life around these moments. He drank alcohol, took medication, or used drugs more often than he had before, telling himself he only needed something to take the edge off enough to get through the evening or sleep through the night. He also became careful to avoid police uniforms or weapons whenever he could, changing the route he took to a café if he thought he might pass officers on the street, and leaving social events early if security staff or law enforcement were visible at the entrance. When he could not avoid contact with reminders, he sometimes lifted both hands to cover his face, pressing his palms over his eyes and forehead in a gesture that seemed to give him a momentary sense of concealment, as though if he could not see the uniforms or the lights, they could not see him either. He knew these habits were narrowing his world. He stopped staying out late, declined invitations to bars and concerts, and began choosing restaurants by how open they felt from the door. His work as a graphic designer, once flexible and social, became more solitary still, with fewer in-person meetings and a growing preference for remote communication. Even then, he found it hard to be fully at ease when a client's building had uniformed security at the entrance or when he had to wait in a lobby where weapons might be visible on a belt.

By the time he sought help, Evan was living with the accumulated weight of these reactions and the loneliness of trying to manage them privately. The divorce had already left him untethered from the routines that once anchored him, and now he felt he was organizing his days around avoiding the dark, avoiding certain cars, and avoiding places where people packed too closely around him. What finally brought him in was the sense that he was no longer just adapting his life but shrinking it. He was tired of needing alcohol or medication just to get through an evening, tired of hiding his face in public when a uniform came into view, and tired of waking in the dark with his heart already racing before he could remember where he was. He said he did not expect to feel safe in the same way he once had, but he hoped he could at least stop feeling as if danger might be waiting at every turn of a parking lot, every familiar-looking car, and every crowded doorway.
